newsitem.title: UK: World awaits FOMC but why are US rates so important?.
newsitem.headline: World awaits FOMC but why are US rates so important?.

text.p: Interest rate moves in the United States are still far and away the most important event for global financial markets, and investors are as usual waiting with bated breath for the outcome of Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
The 12-member policy committee of the U.S. Federal Reserve meets eight times a year, around every six weeks or so, to set its policy stance.
In other words whether the central bank, after taking into account the pace of growth and the level of inflation, will maintain the status-quo or tighten or loosen its grip on credit.
But why are U.S. rates so important for the rest of the world, and in particular financial markets?
The simple answer is that the U.S. is still the world's locomotive for growth and its bond market is the world's largest and most important financial market.

"Movements in global financial markets are heavily correlated," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London. "Quite simply the U.S. is the world's largest economy so developments there affect us all either directly or indirectly."
The link comes through two angles.
The first is the currency effect should the dollar, the world's reserve currency, move significantly after a rate change.
For example, the dollar may rally after a U.S. rate rise and if a country's currency weakens significantly it could start to 'import' inflation via more expensive dollar denominated imports.
Remember, the majority of the world's raw materials such as oil are priced in dollars.
A threatened rise in inflation via a weaker currency could well prompt a government to raise rates to counter the inflationary impact of a weaker currency.
The second link is the impact a rate change has on U.S. growth, in other words the economic locomotive effect.
If the locomotive slows down because rates have been raised or speeds up if rates are cut, the countries who are the 'wagons' slow down or speed up accordingly.
While it is true that producers tend to go and set up shop in the United States if that is their biggest export market, it is nevertheless still a massive market for many overseas producers.
Although policy makers in other countries may be forced to act on rates after a change in U.S., they do have the luxury of waiting to see just what impact there is.

Financial markets on the other hand not only try to anticipate the impact it might have, so they can make money on instruments like financial futures, but they are also influenced by what has happened in the past.
"This is why financial markets react more quickly and tend to read a lot more into things than policy makers who can wait and see what the impact is on their domestic economies," Lyons said.
So what is going to happen on Tuesday? Unfortunately the experts are divided but after inflation figures that were a little higher than expected, analysts are tending to lean towards a rate rise.
"The markets, up until the end of last week, were of the opinion that U.S rates weren't going to go up," said Jeremy Stretch, currency strategist at NatWest markets.

But looking at the Dow's fall on Friday and the underlying CPI numbers being a little higher than expected have made the market stop and think a little bit that it's no longer a one-way bet. I think it's a close call, one way or the other."
